title: Two Jobs in One Green Cell

scenes.tts: How can one green leaf cell build sugar and release energy from it? Watch one large cell stay on screen as its parts begin working. Its two jobs use different cell parts, but their materials connect.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: photosynthesis and chloroplast green; respiration and mitochondrion red; oxygen and water blue; light and energy yellow; carbon dioxide and labels grey. Fill most of the frame with one green leaf cell. A green chloroplast and red mitochondrion sit dimly inside. Slow cytoplasm particles drift. A question mark grows between the two organelles as arrows begin to trace an unfinished loop. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: How can one green leaf cell build sugar and release energy from it? Watch one large cell stay on screen as its parts begin working. Its two jobs use different cell parts, but their materials connect.

scenes.visual: Keep the same living cell moving gently in the background. Bring in the title 'Two Jobs in One Green Cell' for two seconds, then shrink it into the upper corner without clearing the cell.

scenes.tts: Sunlight reaches the cell, and a green chloroplast swells into view. A chloroplast is a cell part that takes in light for photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide and water move inside. Sugar, called glucose, and oxygen move out.
scenes.visual: Zoom toward the green chloroplast while keeping the cell edge visible. Yellow rays sweep in from the upper left. Grey 'carbon dioxide' and blue 'water' blocks enter. Transform them inside the chloroplast into a green 'sugar' block and blue oxygen bubbles that travel outward. Keep all blocks schematic and labelled.
scenes.narration: Sunlight reaches the cell, and a green chloroplast swells into view. A chloroplast is a cell part that takes in light for photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide and water move inside. Sugar, called glucose, and oxygen move out.

scenes.tts: The sugar does not sit still. It moves toward a red mitochondrion, another cell part. Most cellular respiration happens in mitochondria. Respiration breaks down the sugar with oxygen, and usable energy comes out. Carbon dioxide and water also leave.
scenes.visual: Pan across the same cell as the green sugar block moves toward the red mitochondrion. Just outside it, split the sugar block into smaller green pieces; the pieces and blue oxygen bubbles then enter. The mitochondrion pulses red. A yellow 'usable energy' arrow moves toward a gently working cell icon. Grey carbon dioxide and blue water blocks exit toward the chloroplast side.
scenes.narration: The sugar does not sit still. It moves toward a red mitochondrion, another cell part. Most cellular respiration happens in mitochondria. Respiration breaks down the sugar with oxygen, and usable energy comes out. Carbon dioxide and water also leave.

scenes.tts: What went in? A reactant is a substance entering a process. What came out? A product is a substance leaving a process. Watch each product badge move to the other cell part, where it becomes a reactant. The products of either process can supply reactants for the other.
scenes.visual: Rebuild both organelles large inside the same cell. Small grey 'reactant' tabs attach to blocks entering each organelle; green 'product' tabs attach as blocks leave. As each block crosses the cell, smoothly flip its tab from 'product' to 'reactant'. Keep the loop moving rather than listing terms.
scenes.narration: What went in? A reactant is a substance entering a process. What came out? A product is a substance leaving a process. Watch each product badge move to the other cell part, where it becomes a reactant. The products of either process can supply reactants for the other.

scenes.tts: Now the sun moves toward the horizon, but the cell still needs usable energy. Which moving arrows will stop after darkness arrives? Keep the chloroplast, mitochondrion, and every material in mind.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole cell. Move a yellow sun along a day-to-night arc. Keep every material arrow moving until the question appears. Freeze all arrows at their current positions while the question shows. Show the question 'Which arrows stop in darkness?' and a quiet countdown ring with no numbers.
scenes.narration: Now the sun moves toward the horizon, but the cell still needs usable energy. Which moving arrows will stop after darkness arrives? Keep the chloroplast, mitochondrion, and every material in mind.

scenes.visual: Hold the question over the same cell for a deliberate thinking pause. Let cytoplasm particles drift and the countdown ring slowly close. Do not reveal which arrows stop.

scenes.tts: Darkness removes the light arrow. The chloroplast stops making new sugar and oxygen. Respiration keeps using stored sugar and oxygen. It keeps releasing usable energy, carbon dioxide, and water. The plant cell is still respiring.
scenes.visual: Turn the background to night. Fade the yellow light arrow and all chloroplast input and output arrows. Split a stored green sugar block into smaller pieces just outside the still-pulsing red mitochondrion, then move the pieces and blue oxygen bubbles inside. Continue yellow usable-energy motion. Let the grey carbon dioxide and blue water from the mitochondrion drift out of the cell edge, not into the chloroplast.
scenes.narration: Darkness removes the light arrow. The chloroplast stops making new sugar and oxygen. Respiration keeps using stored sugar and oxygen. It keeps releasing usable energy, carbon dioxide, and water. The plant cell is still respiring.

scenes.tts: Light returns, and photosynthesis starts making new sugar and oxygen again. Respiration continues at the same time. A green leaf cell does not switch between jobs. It can photosynthesize and respire while light is available. Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night.
scenes.visual: Move the sun back above the horizon. Restore the yellow light arrow and green chloroplast motion without stopping the red mitochondrion. Run both sets of arrows together. Briefly label both organelles, then let the labels settle beside them.
scenes.narration: Light returns, and photosynthesis starts making new sugar and oxygen again. Respiration continues at the same time. A green leaf cell does not switch between jobs. It can photosynthesize and respire while light is available. Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night.

scenes.tts: Follow the material badges around the cell. Carbon dioxide and water can help build sugar and oxygen. Sugar and oxygen can then feed respiration. Matter can be used again. Energy takes a different path through the picture.
scenes.visual: Emphasize the closed-looking material route with moving grey, blue, and green labelled blocks. Keep an opening at the cell edge to show matter can also enter or leave. Dim the yellow energy arrow until the final sentence, then brighten it as a separate path.
scenes.narration: Follow the material badges around the cell. Carbon dioxide and water can help build sugar and oxygen. Sugar and oxygen can then feed respiration. Matter can be used again. Energy takes a different path through the picture.

scenes.tts: Yellow light enters once. Chemical energy travels with the sugar, then becomes energy the cell can use. Some energy leaves as heat. The matter arrows loop, but energy flows one way.
scenes.visual: Send one continuous yellow ribbon from sunlight to the sugar block, then through the mitochondrion to 'usable energy'. Let the ribbon thin and drift out as yellow heat waves. Keep the material blocks circulating behind it. Add a one-way arrowhead to the energy ribbon.
scenes.narration: Yellow light enters once. Chemical energy travels with the sugar, then becomes energy the cell can use. Some energy leaves as heat. The matter arrows loop, but energy flows one way.

scenes.tts: Move back outside the leaf. The same two jobs help explain oxygen in a pond or creek. Photosynthetic organisms add oxygen only while light is available. Plants, animals, fungi, and many microbes use oxygen through respiration. That use continues in darkness.
scenes.visual: Zoom out from the cell into a leaf, then a simple creek bank. Carry the blue oxygen bubbles and the green/red concept colors through the zoom. Place small schematic grass, algae, animal, fungus, and microbe icons around moving blue bubbles. A day-night arc advances toward darkness.
scenes.narration: Move back outside the leaf. The same two jobs help explain oxygen in a pond or creek. Photosynthetic organisms add oxygen only while light is available. Plants, animals, fungi, and many microbes use oxygen through respiration. That use continues in darkness.

scenes.tts: In light, oxygen can be added. Through day and night, respiration keeps using it. Carry that pattern into ponds and creeks.
scenes.visual: Reduce the creek to two moving arrows: green oxygen addition under a yellow sun, and red oxygen use spanning the full day-night bar. Let both arrows settle into the exact end-card sentence before the screen clears.
scenes.narration: In light, oxygen can be added. Through day and night, respiration keeps using it. Carry that pattern into ponds and creeks.

scenes.visual: Show one line only, centered at large size: 'Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night.' No title, subtitle, icon, or smaller line.
